speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head K of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Education, when done well, is an avenue of social mobility, a social multiplier, a maximiser of human potential, a character builder, a wealth creator and a passport to countless life’s opportunities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although these ITMs differ in scope, depth and quality, they share a common value-add.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The mapping exercise "forces" industry captains to study the current and future landscape, review their vision and, in the process, help the rest of the industry and Singapore to understand, support and partake in their future directions, priorities, jobs and skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The missing piece is for the years between early childhood and adult education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is merit for MOE to put together an overall Education Transformation Map.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Granted, there are news on developments and priorities when MOE chooses to announce either through Ministerial Statements or its annual workplans, but the overall Education Map needs to be developed and articulated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to see a map that consolidates the overall vision, the future of education, the developments, the current state of the union, risk assessment, the key pieces it needs to eyeball and move, the challenges and how it can better engage other stakeholders in its work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot ignore the larger elephants in the room, such as the still growing and increasingly market-responsive tuition industry and the continuing excessive focus on the academic rat race.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot keep tweaking the system and hope that age-old mindsets and habits will disappear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them cannot be solved by MOE's think-tank alone.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to be bold enough to honestly ask what our education system should look like and decide where we should redesign, reskill and better resource.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On vision of education, the fast pace of technology has led to an increasingly shorter shelf life of our knowledge and skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Staying relevant through lifelong learning is an essential part of life and no longer a luxury.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, the SkillsFuture movement is a brilliant strategy but it is now focused primarily on adults and, at most, students in the IHLs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the cultivation of curiosity in learning, self-driving one's learning, digital literacy and learning agility must start young.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is, therefore, a need to integrate and align SkillsFuture in the adult years with SkillsFuture in the junior years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us be the first in the world to build the first "Lifelong Learning Schools".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us re-envision MOE as a Ministry of Lifelong Learning and to seriously study what that vision truly means and entails.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on benchmark of education, for years, Singapore has prided ourselves in our outstanding performance in global education rankings, such as the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) study.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: PISA ranks our 15-year-olds globally in subjects, such as Reading, Math, Science and Problem Solving – factors viewed as important for boosting economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although a good reference point, I believe Singapore can lead and establish a more comprehensive suite of education benchmarks.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For one, we know we have to now learn for life beyond the age of 15.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, surely, we, too, agree that the purpose of education is more than just to prepare economic beings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What about citizenship, compassion, learning agility, curiosity, regional and world languages and culture and the courage to take risks?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What about the sense of duty to look after one's family, to respect other people who are different, protect our environment, including cleaning up after ourselves?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask MOE, as we expand our old definition of education and success, I wish to seek resources for the Ministry to conduct a uniquely Singapore study of the benchmarks against which to measure the success of our education system Next, on engine of education, our educators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Amongst all, one key engine of education must be our Educators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have and still serve with some of the most dedicated, competent and compassionate educators, and I feel for them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to nurture and maximise the potential of our staff, too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The days of old when teachers are the key dispensers of knowledge and principals are leaders who know all about education, are over.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, the term "teacher" may need to be dropped soon as educators take on the roles of creators and/or curators of content, designers of learning experiences, facilitators and coaches of their students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They need to be exposed not only to things of the school, but also to the world that their students are going to live and work in.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They themselves, the educators, too, need to be mentally healthy and coached.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What are the ways by which MOE educators, including school leaders, are recruited and developed to fulfil the roles of future educators?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can we future-proof them through updating and innovating the ways by which they are recruited and developed?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on inclusiveness of education, any map of education is incomplete without including those who are at risk of being left out either due to their socio-economic background or their learning styles and abilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On digital literacy for all, many future of education studies reflect everywhere that digital literacy is the new literacy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As mobile devices become commonly used for learning, students without the financial means may be left out.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In situations, such as the COVID-19 outbreak, when students are expected to stay home with e-learning, with blended homework packages, those without access to ready IT devices may be deprived.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides devices, there are also students who may be left behind in the chase of acquisition for digital literacy due to little access or exposure to digital content or sufficient learning exposure either at home or in school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On student with Special Education Needs (SEN), thanks to the political leaders and several key Ministries, such as the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and MOE, the education of students with SEN, especially for the young, has grown from strength to strength.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the outcomes of their schooling will need a deeper dive for further improvement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To this end, I seek MOE's favourable consideration for three groups of students with SEN.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is to enhance the chances that more of them will be more prepared for life after school, the formal school years, and for more of them to work in at least supported employment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them are not ready to exit to the adult world at the age of 18.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The alternative is to put them in costly day activity centres for adults or for parents to give up their own livelihoods in order to care for them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, for students with SEN who are able to undertake mainstream subjects whether in primary schools, secondary schools or IHLs, MOE should articulate and implement a more effective plan so that they are better supported.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Failing to do so will incur not only further expenditure in future budgets, but we, as a society, would also be for the weaker when we leave them behind.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, provide stronger support to the lifelong learning of students with SEN in all settings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many subjects which a student learns in school may not be relevant years later because of new discoveries and technological developments.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Yet, many students and their parents continue to obsess over the need to learn to pass exams.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Students worry about their academic performance in schools.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This has led to unnecessary stress on the students.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the past years, during the Edusave Awards ceremony, I urge parents to work with the school teachers to inculcate the joy of learning in their children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The students should not be caught up in trying to memorise their textbooks just to score better results.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Instead, they ought to be given exposure to discovering new things and finding out more about topics in which they are interested in.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Learning must be for life because the world keeps changing and developing over the years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I first started legal practice, I had to learn how to use a Phillips word processor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I then attended classes to learn how to use Wordstar and Word Perfect.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If I did not keep learning, I would not be able to manage without knowing Microsoft Office today.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know that MOE wants to encourage the students to appreciate that education should be a lifelong journey.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But it is not enough for MOE to say so.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The school teachers must buy in and not add stress onto the students by having a continuous stream of tests and exams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had the opportunity to review the speech of Minister Ong Ye Kung made in 2018 when he held out elderly learners from our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations imbibed with the "lifelong learning" attitudes as great examples for our children to follow and build resilience in a fast-changing global economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One such example is Mr Albert Chang, aged 70.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When he was 14 years old, he left Queenstown Secondary School to work and take care of his family consisting of six siblings, including himself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He joined the Naval Base, which was still managed by the British then, as an electrical engineering apprentice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After the British withdrawal, he became a weapons specialist with Singapore Electronic and Engineering Limited (SEEL), one of the two companies that took over the base and which later merged with Singapore Technologies (ST).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Eager to upgrade himself, he attended night classes after work at the Lembaga which was set up in 1960 to promote adult education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He passed his GCE "O" level exams through this route.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On his own, he pursued a City and Guilds of London Institute course and was issued with a Full Technological Certificate in electrical engineering practice specialising in instruments in 1972.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One memorable project he undertook was the installation of the cable car system from Mount Faber to Sentosa as a Project Manager.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: During the recession, engineering jobs dried up, he was made redundant, he joined the insurance industry.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was not his comfort zone but he was determined to give it his best shot.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He then, through self-study, became a Chartered Life Underwriter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, engineering remained his first love, so he went back.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the mid-2000s, he pursued a Double Masters in Project Management and Risk Management.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is still attending courses and presentations at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is now focusing on upgrading his information technology (IT) knowledge, learning Python and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The values and attitudes of Mr Chang and the people of his generation were shaped by Singapore's —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali Pillai, could you wrap up, please?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: — Singapore's humble economic circumstances in the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, it seems to me that the only thing which is constant about the world is that everything will change at some point.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Indeed, the rate of change we are experiencing gets quicker and quicker every year.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: For example, by some estimates, the amount of data in the world doubles every two years.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: The difficulty we face is how we get our youths ready for the future when we do not know for certain what the future holds.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: If we do not know what the future is going to look like, then it makes it immensely difficult to predict the skills that will be needed for the future.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: But what is clear is that we need our youths to be resilient, adaptable and have a global outlook.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: To keep pace with changes in the world, we must teach our youths to keep an open mind and to be willing to learn and relearn throughout their lives.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In short, we need to make lifelong learning second nature for our youths.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: That seems to be the most effective way to make the next generation of Singaporeans ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister share what steps are being taken to encourage our youths to learn for life?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I am interested, however, to hear what the experiences of the 28 pilot schools are and how they have found the move to FSBB.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister give an update on the pilot and how successful or otherwise this has been?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Quality education should be accessible to all Singaporeans, regardless of family background.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is a multiracial, multicultural country with unique history and characteristics.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since Independence, the bilingual policy has been the cornerstone of our education system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It helps different races to communicate with one another and also plays an indispensable role in promoting cohesion and harmony within the society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, language, as a tool of communication, is only one part of its functions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is underpinned by culture, which is the key feature of a nation and a key achievement of human civilisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In order to have a deeper understanding of our culture and reinforce our identity, a firm grasp of our mother tongue is key.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With rapid globalisation, Singaporeans must continue to have a good grasp of two languages and two cultures and even more languages to stay ahead.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will enhance the competitiveness of Singaporeans internationally and help strengthen Singapore's role as an economic and cultural bridge between different parts of the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, a good grasp of our mother tongue is beneficial for our personal development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Researchers have found that learning two languages can stimulate our mental development, especially for children learning multiple languages at a young age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Benefits for these children include improved cognitive ability, concentration and memory, and greater flexibility when the brain needs to switch between mental tasks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The variety of vocabulary and expressions in different languages also affects our ability to gain insights about the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: People who speak multiple languages have a more enriched understanding of the world compared to monolingual individuals.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our country's bilingual policy has undergone several reforms, and has laid a good language foundation for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this regard, what are MOE’s new measures to nurture even more bicultural talents?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Because this is a cut on Mother Tongue, let me try to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It is going to be a terrible experience, speaking after the eloquent Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: (In Mandarin):   When I was young, I did not speak Mandarin very often, partly because my parents spoke Hokkien to me at home and my brothers and sisters only spoke to me in English.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: When I was studying law in the university, I read the English law papers every day.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It was a cause of regret for me when I graduated because I did not have a good grasp of my mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: When I try to speak Mandarin to my clients, they would say "It is better that you speak English." When I joined the grassroots organisations, I discovered that if I spoke Mandarin more frequently, I could grasp it, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: (In English): Let me now try to speak in English so that MOE officers can understand what I say.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This is partly because my parents spoke to me in Hokkien at home and my siblings speak to me in English.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: When I was studying in the university, it was worse because hardly anyone spoke Mandarin at all.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It is a cause of regret for me when I graduated because I did not have a good grasp of my mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I could not speak Mandarin well to my clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But later, when I joined the grassroots organisations, I realised that the more you speak, the more you get confidence in speaking the mother tongue.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Would it be better for the students to have a nurturing environment at home or would it be better to have more specialist schools, where the students can be immersed in an environment where more classmates speak the mother tongue?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I also understand that the school curriculum needs to reflect a balance of many different priorities.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But it is precisely because of this that I call for its inclusion.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And I do so in different years at our Budget discussions because teaching all our schoolchildren Bahasa Melayu speaks to many of our enduring values and our hopes that are reflected in successive Budgets – economic development through regional cooperation, building a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It will also protect and preserve our multiculturalism and promote national integration and a sense of identity rooted in our geography and our history.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) is an integral part of our education system, complementing our academic subjects with a more value-centric and action-based approach to understanding ourselves and the community and the society we live in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is timely that MOE reviews the CCE syllabus.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As MOE does so, I would like to oﬀer three suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our young students need to be provided with a safe space to discuss issues that may have an impact on their mental health and wellness, such as coping with loss or death in the family, appropriate and inappropriate relationships, bullying among friends, social discrimination or domestic violence.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are diﬃcult issues and I would not expect all our school teachers to be professionally equipped to address them or help students manage these issues well.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it would be useful to have social workers and trained school counsellors work closely with our school teachers to help young students who may be facing these issues.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such lessons serve as important reminders to our young students about how our personal hygiene practices can have significant and far-reaching impact on the community we live in and on society at large.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, when we are ill, it is important to maintain good personal hygiene and exercise social responsibility by minimising going out in public, not sneezing or coughing without due care and maintaining social distancing with others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, our personal and community values shape our social responsibility.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, self-centredness and a lack of empathy for others mean we only think of ourselves and make us less "others-centric".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is understandable for each of us to want to protect our personal interests and needs, we can still do so and yet look out for others, show our care for them and extend help where needed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, we know that values are more often caught rather than taught.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know that schools are already doing this.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than involving parents in some learning activities to be done at home with their children, parents who have been actively involved in serving the community, doing volunteer work or actively contributing to society can be invited to share their experience and work with a class of students in school.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These parents serve as significant adults who can positively influence and shape the mindsets of our young students, which can be important for students who may not always have the best role models at home.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing the details of how MOE intends to review and enhance the teaching of CCE in our schools.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, CCE has always been at the heart of Singapore's education system.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In CCE, our students learn to be responsible to family and community, and understand their role in shaping the future of our nation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The current syllabus was implemented in 2014 and, ever since, there has been new emerging trends and global developments that can impact our society.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last year, the Minister for Education shared that educators expend much effort to continuously improve and refine the curriculum and to make it more engaging, relatable and effective.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, I believe that CCE is an important part of our education.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some students, however, think that CCE is a chore or, worse, think that is merely propaganda.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, they do not appreciate its relevance, especially if examinations are around the corner.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider how to make CCE more engaging and robust.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One way is to draw from current happenings to start discussions in CCE lessons.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For instance, teachers can engage students to reflect on the challenges posed by the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak and discuss how best our communities can respond.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Students can discuss how everyone can play a part in being socially responsible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is especially relevant when one of the students in a top school was infected with COVID-19 last week.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When we include more of such relatable content, CCE lessons can become less of a chore to our students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It would also enable teachers to more effectively guide students towards making sound moral judgements and be motivated to contribute to society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is particularly so in light of how the world economy is changing and how more basic types of intellectual work are increasingly going to be handled by technology.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, as I referred to in my Budget speech, the authors of the World Economic Forum Global Competitiveness Report 2019 commented that Singapore has room for improvement in developing skills like critical thinking among its workforce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going forward, clarity about the sources of knowledge and higher level thinking are going to be key.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One aspect of critical thinking which I want to focus on for this cut is conscious reflection on thinking, thought processes, the rules of logic and the principles of knowledge, how we know something is true and the various categories of knowledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important that our students are encouraged to think about thinking itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, they should know how to reduce an argument to its basic form to separate the premises from the conclusion to understand what the tautological statement is to understand the difference between causation and correlation and to be familiar with the various forms of reasoning like the deductive and inductive methods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the IB website, this is described as aiming to make students aware of the interpretative nature of knowledge, including personal ideological biases, "to reflect critically on diverse ways of knowing and on areas of knowledge; to be aware of themselves as thinkers, encouraging them to become more acquainted with the complexity of knowledge." The most central question the TOK addresses is, "How do we know?", while other questions include: "What counts as evidence for X?", "How do we judge which is the best model of Y?", "What does Theory Z mean in the real world?" Some elements of this are covered in the Upper Secondary English curriculum, but not all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This goes beyond language and media literacy, and it is really about the philosophy of knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my speech in the debate on the President's Address in 2018, I mentioned that our CCE syllabus then focused on classroom and theoretical knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I said, "Our young people should walk the talk and we should seed the caring hearts of our next generation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Let them adopt a kindergarten, old folks home, pet shelters and the responsibility of caring for others." It is important that we look into how we can develop age-appropriate strategies for students at different ages so as to increase the effectiveness of CCE in schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share if MOE has been looking into this?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: To strike a chord with students, CCE should also be easily relatable to the students' experiences.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Therefore, is it possible for CCE lessons to be conducted beyond classrooms and even more actively utilise the life experiences of the teachers so that the lessons could be more authentic?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have to inculcate green values in our younger generation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our schools can play a big and important role in educating our students on the importance of Green initiatives and the perils of global warming.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They should also be better informed of the sciences and policies in relation to climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We should make it part of the compulsory curriculum.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Schools can also take the lead in the reduction of single-use plastics and instill a recycling mindset, including handing down used textbooks and using recycled textbooks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share what MOE has done so far and whether MOE can consider embedding sustainability into the curriculum?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like Miss Cheng Li Hui, I would like to ask if there will be changes to increase awareness of climate change and the human impact on both the environment and nature.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This awareness should also be balanced with an acknowledgement of the economic and other constraints that we face, as well as being mindful of the limited impact that we can make as a small country.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, mental health issues are silent, invisible killers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hence, the rising rates of mental health issues among our children and youths are an urgent national challenge and priority.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are many possible causes that may exacerbate the mental health issues, such as academic-based like homework, examinations and projects, or relationship-based like friendship and bullying.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The rise of social media has also created self-image issues that have led many to have unrealistic expectations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: (a) destigmatise mental health issues and increase the number of counsellors in the schools.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Make seeing the school counsellor mandatory for all students, instead of only referring those who are suspected of mental health issues to the school counsellors; (b) integrate mental health as part of co-curricular activities (CCAs) and physical fitness programmes into the schools and rename it as Total Fitness Programme; (c) introduce mindfulness and meditation classes to all schools and equip our young Singaporeans with useful skills to deal with stress for life; (d) strengthen our cyber wellness programme in schools and equip our young Singaporeans with skills and knowledge to deal with the cyber jungle; and (e) further enhance CCE.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The current occasional talks in schools on mental wellness are clearly insufficient and are only scratching the surface.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope MOE can seriously look into this urgent national challenge and consider the measures proposed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, shifts in the global economic centre of gravity towards Asia present immense opportunities for our people.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore is well-placed to leverage opportunities from fast-growing Asia, in particular, Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many Singapore companies see Asia as its marketplace, given the limited growth opportunities in our small domestic market.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, to prepare our future generation to be Asia-ready, I am really happy that we are reviewing our school curriculum to enable students to develop a deeper understanding of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), China and India.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can this new programme provide our students with the opportunity to develop deep insights into the Asian economies and their ways of working and living?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I certainly hope this Programme will not just stop at being an overseas trip to the region.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Indeed, the programme should instead encompass student involvement in community service engagement with the respective Asian communities, working in close collaboration with foreign embassies and student exchange programmes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, I have two young staff in their late 20s who are working for me.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since then, I have worked with them very closely on different projects.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And because my companies, we build our offices regionally, so I empower both of them to take on some of those projects.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I must say that the two of them have a lot of promises, and one of the common things I found was that they are very comfortable discussing about developments in Asia and being very resourceful about getting certain things done, even if it is beyond Singapore's shores.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, countries we talked about are China, Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am quite pleased with their performance but I know it is hard to keep them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the common things I found was that they were exposed to cultural exchange programmes way back in school, starting from secondary school.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I will credit that as the first exposure on a regional basis that makes them feel comfortable in their working life later on.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of them actually had an internship overseas as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This 	Asia-Ready Exposure Programme, if it can go beyond just cultural understanding and differences, it would really help to make that leap forward, and that leap forward is going beyond understanding about the culture, appreciating the culture, but to be able to make that leap into something more.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And that something more, I will look at it this way – three points, on mindset change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And a mindset change creates a certain attitude towards the region and the dare to venture abroad.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After learning about a culture, learn to apply that within the workforce or within their scope of work in future and to take on additional responsibilities from there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And, of course, hopefully, they are all willing to venture abroad.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And that is the part I find it the hardest to persuade.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe it is the comfort of Singapore as well that they are unable or unwilling to really venture abroad on a longer-term basis to actually see what is out there, broaden their horizon.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is extremely important because if we want to do an	Asia-Ready Exposure Programme, we might have to think beyond just understanding of cultures.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But have the schools take them on in the beginning to understand that and then offer it later that they can actually intern overseas as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Give them a chance to do so, so that, in future, Singaporeans will be more competitive, not just in Singapore, but overseas as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This comes on the heels of measures already announced this year and last year for enterprises to take advantage of business opportunities in fast-growing Asia and, more specifically, ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would suggest that less rigorously spoken ASEAN language courses be extended to interested students, including students from IHLs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Such measures, I believe, will greatly facilitate the students' learning experience and enhance job opportunities for them in the ASEAN region.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Chairman, in helping our citizens navigate their way through numerous online falsehoods and fake news, we have to start our public education campaign upstream and begin with our school students.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Beyond community initiatives, we also need to equip our school students with digital literacy, as well as information literacy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Digital and information literacy are the ability to use information and communication technologies to find, evaluate, create and communicate information, requiring both cognitive and technical skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: This combined set of literacies is crucial in this current age, as our students should not only know how to use new information and communication technologies but, more importantly, know how to source for, evaluate and use information that is disseminated and accessed, regardless of the medium in which it exists.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Hence, as MOE reviews the school curricula and syllabi in order to incorporate teaching and learning activities for digital readiness, I would like to propose two areas for consideration.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: One, digital and information literacy should be part of our school syllabi, taught and learnt within a specific subject or as part of a school project.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Digital and information literacy essentially involve applied skills and knowledge.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Here, I must declare my interest as Special Adviser to the DIL-CoP.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Two, in order to facilitate the learning of digital and information literacy, the access to and use of information and communication technologies have to be in place.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: As such, students need to have ready access to and use of technological devices, such as laptops, tablets, and smart phones, all with Internet access and wireless fidelity capabilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What support and provision will be made available?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I look forward to hearing the details of how digital and information literacy will be implemented in our schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Chairman, digital technologies have progressed tremendously and are very much part of our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: They could allow us to achieve more than ever before if we are able to harness their potential and use them wisely with good purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Cybercrimes and online scams have been on the rise and it is not surprising, with the majority of Singaporeans accessing the Internet everyday across different platforms.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In 2016, I filed an MOE cut on cyber education.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Our children are tech-savvy, but they may or may not be Internet-savvy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: They may forget there are real dangers lurking in the cyberspace.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Cyberbullying, online predators and online scams are just some of the dangers youths face.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It is important that we introduce and equip our young Singaporeans with digital literacy in schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: We have made a good start and laid a strong foundation over the last few years when schools started allowing students to use tablets in class.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: This allows for a more enriching classroom experience where learning is now more interactive, interesting and personal.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Will the Ministry also be developing guides or courses for teachers to impart and deepen digital literacy among their students in schools?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: We need to better prepare young Singaporeans for an increasing number of sectors that require advanced AI-related competencies, such as digital finance and cybersecurity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Can the Minister share what is in the pipeline to deepen digital capabilities, especially in our IHLs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, please allow me to declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of ComfortDelGro Taxi business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Over the last decade, digital technology, including but not limited to mobile phone applications technology, has significantly impacted on our daily life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Digital technology has disrupted many business models but has also created new business models.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In ComfortDelGro Taxi business, we have embarked on digital transformation since 2018.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Many technology-based companies and companies that are embarking in digital transformation are finding it hard to recruit local ICT talents in the areas of data analytics, artificial intelligence, automation and other cutting-edge technologies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Moving ahead, are the local universities planning to produce even more ICT graduates?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How are our local universities equipping the non-IT undergraduates with skillsets to interpret data and basic ICT skills so that they can better survive in this digital world?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For that matter, how is MOE developing plans to better equip students from primary to secondary schools to be digital-ready?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Our educators are at the frontline where they deal directly with the students for many of their formative years to impart knowledge, share experience and, most importantly, lead by example.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Therefore, supporting our teachers is key to developing and sustaining a good education system in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: With new developments and trends in the education field, such as the increasing use of e-learning, computational skills and inquiry-based learning, we need to stand ready to ensure that our teachers and educators stay ahead of the curve.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It is an important and never-ending process so that our teachers are well-equipped to nurture future-ready learners.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Can the Minister share how will MOE support the professional development of our teachers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, Sir, youth suicides seem to be on the rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOE and MSF were very concerned with the spike, though both Ministries noted that it was not a trend yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Obviously, we do not want this to become a trend as lives are at stake here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to do more than to closely monitor the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time that youth suicides are on the rise, we see more young people talking about mental illness and turning to Mental Health Services for help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am aware that there are initiatives, such as the Youth Corps programme, to mobilise volunteers to provide peer support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are also many community initiatives responding to the impending youth mental health crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to tackle mental health issues upstream and this is why I am bringing this up under the MOE heading because our schools and IHLs are the headwaters of this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not just that the stress of school work creating anxieties and problems with self-worth, but young people are so caught up in social relationships and the search for identity in the setting of schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A lot of the initiatives on the ground now are oriented towards creating awareness of the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is important as we need to correct persistent prejudices and ignorance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the reasons for the jump in young people seeking help is that they are starting to open up mental health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time for us to listen to young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could learn from other jurisdictions, such as Scotland, which has established a Youth Commission on Mental Health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It comprises young people from ages 16 to 25 to make recommendations to the government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To ensure that we continue to have these positive outcomes, it is imperative that we provide strong support to allow our teachers to deepen their skills and expertise as part of their professional development.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With respect to how professional development is conducted, I have received feedback from teachers that attending courses per se would not necessarily result in a positive classroom impact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The courses should also be tailored and differentiated in accordance with the experience of teachers, subject, ability of students and the specific strengths of the teachers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It would also be good for a ground-up approach to be employed, allowing teacher leaders to find out what is required by his unit and then collaborate with and hold peer discussions on the areas identified.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These leaders should also be able to reach out to resources for help outside their school, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If that happens, the teacher will have to conduct a make-up lesson or get someone to cover him or her.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Perhaps, an appropriate number of days should be set aside from the outset for professional development so that such time would be taken into account in the teacher’s schedule.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This will also manifest a tangible investment in our teachers' professional development.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Chairman, since the introduction of SkillsFuture in 2015, there have been numerous initiatives and programmes launched to ensure Singaporeans have access to a whole spectrum of training and learning opportunities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: While there are SkillsFuture schemes meant for working adults to ensure their continued employability, such as P-Max Place-and-Train and the Professional Conversion Programmes (PCP), there are also Train-and-Place SkillsFuture initiatives targeted at students to prepare them for the workforce, such as the Work-Study Diploma or Degree programmes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The recent Budget announcement by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat gave us a sneak into the Next Bound of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Will there be plans to recognise training courses or certifications to allow them to be stackable components or modules leading to accredited or recognised qualifications that can lead to career promotions or better employment opportunities?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I look forward to hearing these details from the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of Wealth Management Institute, a training provider.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The SkillsFuture movement received a boost of support in this year’s Budget with generous SkillsFuture Credits.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So far, the inertia in take-up can be attributed partly to perceived relevance of SkillsFuture courses and the challenges faced by mid-career workers in navigating the thousands of courses available.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: For the next phase of the SkillsFuture movement, more focus should be placed on building strong connections between employability and Continuing Education and Training (CET) courses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: In the process, they can also be directed to career coaches for support and guidance on their learning journey to better understand career prospects in the identified sectors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: There should be strong incentives for CET providers to establish links between their training courses and on-the-job performance and employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The initiative to identify up to 40 large anchor enterprises to support training for their sectors and value chain partners is, indeed, very timely.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: This initiative can potentially transform the entire supply chain, helping to raise the skills of workers in small and medium enterprises (SMEs) which form an integral part of the supply chain.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Work-study pathways can only be successful with strong industry partnership, commitment on the part of employers and their management teams to make workplace learning meaningful and impactful.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: What plans are in the pipeline to build that necessary infrastructure and ecosystem for impactful work-study programmes?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: What support will companies receive to enable their effective participation in work-study programmes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Post-Secondary Education Account (PSEA) is a useful mechanism for young individuals to help defray the cost of their education.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I am perplexed by the strict limitations placed on PSEA usage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a recent Parliamentary answer, MOE has said that the Ministry was concerned about the quality of the courses, the relevance to the industry and the outcomes to the graduates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although this is fair enough, it should be remembered that we are talking here about an individual's account balances, and not about subsidies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I recently came across a resident who needed to use his PSEA funds for a course in an aeronautical university that has collaborations with the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore, the Air Force and Singapore Airlines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With such extensive local industry partnerships, quality and industry relevance should be less of a concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The resident was in the final year of his course when his father, who sponsored his studies, died suddenly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As his father had remarried, the funding for his studies was abruptly cut off after his death.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He had hoped that MOE would enable him to tap on the more than $3,000 balance in his PSEA to pay for his remaining course fees, but this was turned down.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Monies that are left unutilised in the PSEA when the account holder turns 31 will be transferred to his CPF Ordinary Account.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although the amount of the balances transferred appears modest, tapping on these sums to complete tertiary studies would be welcomed, especially for those less well-off.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of them are mature workers who could not get back into the workforce after losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thus, the concerns of workers are relatively the same, whichever economy they are in.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, while we are advocating lifelong learning for our salaried workers to remain relevant in a changing world, we should do likewise for workers in the gig economy, in particular, the mature workers, so that they, too, can have a decent shot at moving up the value chain while earning their keep as freelancers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am particularly concerned about mature gig workers because ageism would have compounded their struggle to get back into a 9-to-5 routine.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Staying in the gig economy could be their only option to make a living for a while.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And the reality is, the longer they remain in the gig economy, the harder it will be for them to find a day job.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, having the right certifications may open doors to better paying gigs which, in turn, may help these mature workers find meaning in life in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Recently, I came across a freelance trainer who wanted to upgrade himself to become a master trainer.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But to get there, this person would need advanced certification, and subsidies for those expensive courses are only made available for sponsored employees.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: That would mean that this person would need to work for a company or find a company that is willing to sponsor him.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This resident is in his early 60s and was running a regional outfit before he was retrenched.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What are the chances of him getting either one of the funding options?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Since gig workers are on their own, can the Ministry look into introducing a surrogate scheme so that these mature workers in the gig economy can take up specialised courses under similar funding models that sponsored employees are currently given?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Member of Parliament Mr Patrick Tay has made a call for the surrogate scheme to be brought back and I second that.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the SkillsFuture programme is a wonderful initiative which provides tangible support for Singaporeans to learn new skills at every stage of their life.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When it was rolled out in 2016, many Singaporeans made good use of the opportunity to pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the event that the COVID-19 outbreak deepens, there might be some workers laid off in the next few months.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many employers, especially our SMEs, are busy dealing with the here-and-now and have limited bandwidth and time to plan for their future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, rapid technological advancements and disruption require them to continually innovate and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their workers need to keep up with the changes, too.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures or incentives does the Ministry have to help our employers develop stronger workplace training capabilities?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One potential benefit from attending similar SkillsFuture training courses is networking among employees in the same industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such opportunities could be a chance for workers and staff from different SMEs to collaborate.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They could share best practices or even form small working groups where they could brainstorm and exchange ideas.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are all developmental opportunities for workers, too.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such collaborations could increase the chances of our SMEs moving up the value chain to become more innovative and competitive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does SkillsFuture have a role in assisting such companies and facilitating industry collaborations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, potential employers would have doubts about the training credentials of applicants and the programmes might eventually lose their value.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also want to ensure that the SkillsFuture Credits are used wisely.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: There will also be more transport subsidies and school meal subsidies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The bursaries for students in polytechnics and autonomous universities would also be increased.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Providing good education to our students will help families break out of the poverty cycle and level out the inequality in society.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The primary question is how to ensure that our students who can qualify to further their education are not deprived of doing so just because they lack the funds.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Is the process for applying for financial assistance cumbersome?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Are school teachers taught to look out for students in need of financial assistance?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Has there been any feedback that students at that age may feel embarrassed to stretch out their hands for financial assistance?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Once we identify those students who require financial help, will we also find out more about whether the families also require Public Assistance or ComCare?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A few SIBs have been launched in the UK and one in Columbia to target skills training towards those who are unemployed, vulnerable and not in education, employment or training.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: With this cut, I would like to suggest exploration of SIBs as a tool that could be used to direct training towards Singaporeans facing employability issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, most programmes tend to focus on highly skilled disciplines, such as finance or technology.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These two facts mean that the benefits of internship and apprenticeship training tend to accrue only to a select segment of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In particular, many beneficiaries of such programmes tend to be highly-educated students or graduates majoring in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM)-related courses and who possess the means to seek, identify and apply to such opportunities.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is substantial evidence that internship and apprenticeship not only contribute to enhanced knowledge transfer and more efficient production but can also play a role in reducing the extent of labour market polarisation which is becoming a growing concern in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, such systems tend to be more successful when operating within the rubric of a larger institutional framework.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such national level institutions help establish the standard roles behind each party's commitment, promote worker-firm matching and encourage the movement of journeyman to other firms once they have completed their formal training.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government has already started in this direction with the Asia-Ready Exposure Programme being introduced at this Budget.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Importantly, by taking the lead in establishing such a nationally-recognised internship framework, it not only enables voluntary, progressive acquisition of certification for future PMETs, but also enables the Government to qualify an apprenticeship culture that opens up the substantial benefits of such experiences to a much wider range of candidates, such as non-academic pursuits like the culinary arts, music and sports, artisanal practices, such as furniture-making and other skilled crafts and professions that rely on experience and on-the-job training rather than book smarts alone.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This allowed the Government to be a stronger advocate for Singaporeans that have ambitions to contribute to that traditionally and deserved sectors of the economy that nevertheless are paths to meaningful middle-class secured jobs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is concerning, as this shows that there is still much to be done for our workforce to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The gap could possibly be with the existing employed workforce who might like to gain in-depth knowledge on new disciplines like data analytics, software engineering, cybersecurity, information security, process automation and more.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We are starting to see that this will be a strategic concern for employers in the very near future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Mr Chairman, the Next Bound of SkillsFuture comes at an opportune moment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The forces of globalisation and technological advances are reshaping industries and jobs at an accelerating pace.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And with new jobs emerging and requirements of existing jobs changing, there is an increasing need for Singaporeans to continue to reskill and upgrade.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Over the years, the Government has put in place many measures to ramp up career transition and reskilling programmes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: However, many of these programmes, such as PCPs, Place-and-Train programme and sector-specific reskilling programmes requiring individuals to be employed first before they are able to access training.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The placement requirement, which is helpful to secure jobs for individuals, may also limit the number who can benefit from training.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In Singapore, where most families have both parents working and not everyone is fortunate to have their grandparents or domestic helper to look after their school-going children, the reliance on after-school care service becomes very important.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This is especially so for low-income families where they are able to benefit from very good subsidies from the Government.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The parents would prefer to send their children to a school-based after-school care service as they do not need to worry about transport between the school and the after-school care service.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: They are also reassured that the child would not only be given meals but there would also be nap-time, playtime and even time set aside for tuition as well as other meaningful learning activities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: However, for parents, finding a place in the school-based after-school care service is not easy because many of the schools do not have sufficient capacity to cater for all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Hence, many school-based after-school care service have a long waiting list.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Then, there are parents whose child may be underperforming and require special care for them to stay on course.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Also, how is the Ministry supporting disadvantaged students in primary schools through the school-based after-school care service and the UPLIFT programme?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Chairman, I am supportive of the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package for locals in their 40s and 50s to help them stay employable.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: What will MOE be doing differently next, compared to current approaches, that would make these career transition programmes for mid-career switchers to be more effective in helping these mature workers with job placement?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: If we do not do things differently by thinking differently, then most likely, we would get the same results and be unable to achieve the desired outcome of the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: In addition, while a lot of efforts have been taken to reach out to mid-career workers and professionals, many are unaware of the help they could receive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is an increasing awareness about the need to monitor the mental health of our young and provide the necessary support that they may need as they navigate through life's challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, mental health is a multifaceted issue that needs to be addressed through different approaches and platforms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that it is important not just for schools, but also parents, peers and the community to play a role as well as make a concerted effort to create awareness and reduce the stigma.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: MOE, however, could play a critical role in coordinating upstream efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Can MOE share and elaborate about its efforts to help students who are in need of mental health support and how it intends to further develop mental health education in schools?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could MOE perhaps do more to leverage social media, the youths' preferred mode of communication, and work towards building an ecosystem within which all stakeholders could work together to aid early detection, encourage students to seek help when needed and provide pervasive and holistic support in and outside school?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These are the aggressions and indignities some of our students suffer in school.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These naming and shaming methods are harsh and destructive, sabotaging our ability to build positive and edifying learning environments.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such tactics humiliate and demoralise poor performers and also create a toxic and competitive environment where peer-to-peer support becomes collateral damage.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that the majority of our teachers undertake their jobs with professionalism, care and dedication.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Google commissioned a study to identify why some of their teams perform better than others.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They found that a consistent feature of their most successful teams was the concept of "psychological safety".

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Psychological safety is the feeling that you will not be humiliated or jeered at for the ideas you propose, for asking questions or admitting to mistakes.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When adopted in the classroom, students have no fear of looking stupid because the entire class knows that asking questions and making mistakes are vital to learning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When students do not enjoy psychological safety in school and, worse, feel stressed and anxious in the presence of teachers who employ harsh classroom tactics, their ability and passion for learning will be extinguished.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As I make this call, I can already hear the keyboard warriors lambasting me for helping to create a generation of strawberries.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I have no doubt that I will attract such comments as, "Attitudes like this will make our kids soft!

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: If they are never scolded, they will never understand failure." I can only conclude that these individuals must have suffered aggressions themselves.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Even in the working world, there is increasing recognition of the importance of psychological safety to improved performance and effective learning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What more, the importance of psychological safety in our schools and classrooms?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that even these teachers who engage in petty aggressions are well-meaning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Their actions are symptomatic of the broader pressures that teachers themselves face in delivering results.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Be that as it may, they must be made to realise that such disparaging treatment of students must be abhorred, that shaming and humiliation can exact a considerable toll on students' self-esteem, and will ultimately kill their interest in learning.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As many of my fellow Members of Parliament have emphasised, issues around the mental health of young people are on the ascent.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Do the teacher preparation curricula in the National Institute of Education's diploma programmes include such training and competency building?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us strive to foster a positive learning environment to ignite the spark for learning, not just for school, but for life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Ministry planning to improve this ratio to better provide first-line mental health support to students?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: MOE currently deploys part-time MOE-trained school counsellors, para-counsellors, Flexi-Adjunct School Counsellors and Teacher Counsellors to augment school counsellors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry clarify on the choice behind deploying these staff instead of directly increasing the number of school counsellors?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One respondent shared that her experience with school counsellors has not been helpful.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I quote, "One completely dismissed me when I told her about my symptoms, and another one recommended exercise as a form of weight loss for someone with an eating disorder." Teachers must have relevant subject matter expertise before attending teacher training at the National Institute of Education (NIE).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I understand that applicants for school counsellors on the "Applicants Without Counselling Training" track need only hold a university degree.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider giving the same value and rigour to the role of counsellors by ensuring that all candidates have appropriate competencies, experience and/or professional qualifications before attending the necessary school-specific training?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry also share how it assesses the competency of school counsellors and how this is aligned with national competency assessment frameworks for counselling professionals?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite a general consensus that early detection leads to better health outcomes, and the need for regular assessment of students' needs and health called by the Health Promoting Schools Framework, free health screenings for students currently focus exclusively on physical health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), half of mental health illnesses start by 14 years of age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, WHO has found that late detection of mental health conditions is known to result in "increased morbidity, mortality and the adoption of life-threatening and life-adopting self-treatments".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As currently practised in schools like Yale-National University of Singapore (NUS) College on admission, will the Ministry consider putting in place mental health screenings every year?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In a whole-child approach, there is no health without mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The screenings are not meant to be diagnostic in purpose, but to increase the channels where teachers, counsellors and parents can identify students who need more help to adopt upstream preventive measures.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this mental health check will better support the engagement and feedback process among teachers, counsellors and parents.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Hence, it is important to give emphasis on what we can do to help children from low-income families in terms of education.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I believe we can do more for Institute of Technical Education (ITE) students because they are at a phase of acquiring important vocational skills.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Could MOE share what further efforts are being taken to enhance financial support for our students, specifically on the bursaries for ITE students?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare that I have a child who is studying in a full-time madrasah.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In 2015, I asked MOE through a Parliamentary Question to consider extending Edusave Awards to madrasah students.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The Minister responded that, "Edusave Awards recognise secular academic and non-academic achievements in the context of MOE-funded schools.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It would not be appropriate to extend awards to private schools, including those in the six full-time madrasahs that offer a total curriculum that comprises both compulsory religious and secular subjects." During 2012's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, another Member and I requested to have the Edusave account and contributions to be extended to Singaporean students who are studying in non-public schools.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: MOE declined this request and explained that the Ministry's policy is to encourage all Singaporean children, as far as possible, to enroll in national schools with the objective to forge social cohesion and a common national identity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Nonetheless, the Prime Minister in his 2013 National Day Rally speech announced that Edusave accounts and contributions would be given to all students of school-going age, which includes full-time madrasah students.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: On MOE's considerations of not awarding Edusave Awards to madrasah students due to madrasah offering a total curriculum that comprises both compulsory religious and secular subjects, this can be addressed by only granting the Edusave Award for secular subjects.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Will the Ministry consider extending the same subsidies and benefits to such students under our United Nations Convention for the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) obligations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, we have been encouraging Singaporean students to upgrade and the Government has also increased the capacity of the institutes of higher learning (IHLs).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: But tuition fees at the IHLs have been on the rise since 2010.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
