text: Last year, Steve from Bukit Merah Secondary started training to be a Peer Support Leader.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He buddied up with his classmate Mark, who was frequently absent due to his gaming addiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Steve encouraged Mark to come to school, and started eating with him during recess and breaks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Steve's friends also joined in, and got to know Mark as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Whenever he could, Steve met with Mark after school to help him with work that he had missed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Gradually, Mark started coming to school more regularly and more punctually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When we asked Mark what helped him to make the change, he said he felt really encouraged when he asked Steve if anyone missed him when he was absent, and Steve replied simply, "Have lah, have lah".

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The smallest, simplest gestures can make a difference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our vision is for every student to be a peer supporter, forming a strong network of support in their class, CCA or peer group, where they can look out for each other and seek guidance from teachers or counsellors where necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) have also put in place peer support programmes similar to those in schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similarly, the Polytechnics and ITEs have worked with the Health Promotion Board to develop mental health resources for their students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Together, we will equip our students with the knowledge, skills and support networks to better overcome challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But even so, there will be a small number of students who struggle with mental health issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For these students, additional support by professionals is needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We need to identify these students in order to support them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Teachers in schools and class advisors in IHLs are trained to pick up signs of distress, reach out to students facing difficulties, and refer them to a counsellor if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With stronger mental health education and peer support cultures, students will also be able to look out for one another and seek guidance from teachers and counsellors if they notice that a friend is struggling.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Students who require additional support will be referred to the counselling professionals in schools, including counsellors and para-counsellors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Students assessed by counsellors to have more serious mental health issues will then be referred to external professionals for further clinical assessment and intervention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To Ms Anthea Ong’s suggestion to increase the number of counsellors, MOE will continue to work with our institutions to review this regularly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, those with higher needs will be able to hire additional counsellors and are given the funding and the manpower provisions to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But counsellors are just one part of the wider eco-system of support for mental well-being in our schools and IHLs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This eco-system, comprising peer support networks, teachers, counsellors, external professionals, provides a robust and responsive approach to ensuring timely identification and targeted intervention for students with mental health needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also need to evaluate the age appropriateness and effectiveness in the school context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To illustrate how our system of support works, let me share another student’s story with you – we will call him Sam.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A few years ago, Sam was suffering from panic attacks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He could not submit his work on time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: His teacher referred him to the school counsellor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The counsellor learnt that Sam’s parents were going through a divorce and that was what was causing Sam to struggle with severe anxiety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The school counsellor taught him coping strategies and worked with mental health professionals to address his anxiety condition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, Sam still found the situation overwhelming and stopped coming to school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They continued working with a Social Service Agency (SSA) to reach out and support Sam and his family.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Sam’s classmates and CCA-mates also encouraged him to return to school, offering a listening ear and help in homework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Over time, Sam started to attend school again and re-joined his CCA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, he has become a peer supporter himself and is using his experience to help others who are going through similar difficulties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, you can see from there it is a whole eco-system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Support for youth mental well-being is a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Outside of MOE, a lot of work is being done by other Government agencies, SSAs, community groups, private organisations and individuals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, our youths themselves should be at the centre of these efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Earlier this year, MSF, MOH and MOE, in collaboration with MCCY and the National Youth Council (NYC), issued an open call to anyone interested in improving youth mental well-being.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Minister Desmond will share more about the network during MSF’s COS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure our education system provides opportunities for all, MOE is also committed to supporting students with Special Educational Needs (SEN) to reach their fullest potential.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Over the years, we have increased the variety of high quality educational settings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, around 80% of students with SEN learn in mainstream schools, supported by teachers and allied educators with specialised skills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our Special Education (SPED) schools, which provide customised learning environments, dedicated resources and specialised manpower, support the remaining 20% of students with higher needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about MOE’s plans to support students with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For students in SPED schools, we are continually improving affordability and accessibility of education.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since January this year, six SPED schools have lowered their fees by at least 25% for Singapore citizens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also working with SSAs to open three new SPED schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One will support students with moderate-to-severe SEN who have both Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Intellectual Disability, while the other two will support students with moderate SEN who have ASD and can access the National Curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While the exit age remains at 18, students offering an academic or vocational national certification may remain in SPED schools until age 21.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will allow them additional time to become work-ready.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Most will progress to open employment before the age of 21.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For students with SEN in mainstream schools, I am happy to announce two new initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, MOE has developed a professional development roadmap to enhance SEN training for all educators in mainstream schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, we will provide more financial assistance to students with SEN in IHLs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Minister announced earlier that MOE will embark on SkillsFuture for Educators or SFEd.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Support for students with SEN is one of the focus areas of SFEd.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have thus developed a new SEN Professional Development Roadmap (PD Roadmap), to better equip our educators in mainstream schools to support students with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want every teacher in mainstream schools to become more skilled in supporting students with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE will work with NIE to strengthen the inclusion of SEN support strategies in pre-service teacher training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For in-service teachers, MOE will launch bite-sized online learning resources in phases from this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The SEN PD roadmap will also provide more professional development (PD) opportunities for educators who play a more specialised role in SEN support – namely, our Allied Educators in Learning and Behavioural Support, teachers trained in Special Needs or (TSNs) as well as the school management team.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE will share more details in the coming months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, MOE will extend the SEN Fund to cater to a wider spectrum of learning needs beyond those with sensory or physical impairments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The SEN Fund was established in 2014 to help Polytechnic and ITE students with physical or sensory impairment to purchase education-related assistive technology (AT) devices and support services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Feedback on the SEN Fund has been positive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In my engagements with students with SEN at the Polytechnics and ITE, they told me it would be helpful to extend the SEN Fund beyond physical disabilities, and they are right, as is Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Advancement in assistive technology devices have made it easier for students with other types of challenges to access education and prepare for independent work and life.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Eligible students can approach their SEN Support Office to apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I am also happy to say that the Autonomous Universities will be extending the same support to their students with SEN for the purchase of assistive technology devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides funding, the SEN Support Offices in our IHLs also provide support to students with SEN from pre-enrolment to graduation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before enrolling in an IHL, prospective students can approach the SEN Support Offices in IHLs to find out more about courses that better suit their interests and learning needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After enrolment, the SEN Support Offices work with the lecturers and tutors to make arrangements to ensure that students with SEN can access the curriculum and assessment tasks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For students with SEN who require additional support to transition to the workplace as an intern, the IHLs also work with SG Enable and SSAs to identify suitable internship opportunities, prepare the students and ensure that they get the support that they need during internship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE will continue to work with schools and IHLs to strengthen support for students with SEN to ensure that they, like all other students, receive the support they need to maximise their potential.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE is also committed to ensuring that financial circumstances are never a barrier to education for Singaporean students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Students with financial difficulties can tap on a variety of MOE support schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another 72,000 students from low- to middle income families in our IHLs benefited from the government bursaries in academic year 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Last year, we announced changes to make preschool and higher education more affordable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure that education remains affordable at every stage, MOE will enhance financial support for two more groups – students on the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme at Primary, Secondary and pre-University levels as well as full-time NITEC and Higher NITEC students in ITE.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister announced this in the Budget Statement and I will provide more details today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, we will enhance the MOE FAS, which supports Singaporean students at the Primary, Secondary and pre-University levels.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means that for parents paying a school bus fare of $110, out-of-pocket fees will drop to $45, which is down from $55 today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The meal subsidy for Primary school students will remain at $2 per meal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These FAS enhancements will be similarly applied to students in the lowest income tier of the MOE Independent School Bursary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOE will also extend applicable aspects of the FAS enhancements to SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Similar to last year, we expect around 52,000 students from the Primary to pre-University levels to benefit from the enhancements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will cost around $52 million each year, a 20% increase from today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, MOE will increase support for full-time NITEC and Higher NITEC students in ITE, which Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Zainal Sapari asked about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, MOE subsidises over 90% of the total cost of NITEC and Higher NITEC courses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Lower and middle income students can receive further assistance through a cash bursary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOE will enhance the cash bursary by between $50 and $200.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is for NITEC and Higher NITEC students from families with gross household income of $2,750 and below, or per capita income of $690 and below.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We expect around 19,000 students to benefit from the enhanced ITE bursaries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Students within the top 10% of GCE "N" or "O" Level entrants in each Higher NITEC and NITEC course receive the Community Development Council/Citizens' Consultative Committee-ITE Scholarship.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These scholars currently receive a cash award of $1,600 a year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: From April 2020, the scholarship will be enhanced to also cover their fees fully.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Around 1,400 NITEC students and 1,200 Higher NITEC students will benefit from this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will also rename the scholarship to ITE Community Scholarship to better reflect its purpose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With these enhancements, we will spend around $28 million a year on bursaries and scholarship for full-time NITEC and Higher NITEC students, an increase of around 20% from today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To ensure that students can easily access financial support schemes, we agree with Mr Lim Biow Chuan that the application process should be simple, without causing any embarrassment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In MOE schools, teachers and staff keep a lookout for students who may require financial assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When approaching students, they take care to do so sensitively and discreetly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOE also partners with Self-Help Groups to support students and families who need additional assistance beyond MOE.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In our IHLs, information on financial aid and application processes is readily available online or can be obtained at the institution's financial aid office.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The process is even simpler for families on ComCare assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Students in our schools, Polytechnics and ITE, whose families are on ComCare assistance will be automatically granted MOE financial assistance without the need for any more documentation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Despite our best efforts, we recognise that there are still some students who struggle in our education system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Each of these students has a unique set of challenging circumstances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We believe that these can be overcome with the right support and that is why we set up UPLIFT – the Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Cheng Li Hui, Mr Charles Chong and Dr Lim Wee Kiak have asked about UPLIFT's work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A key focus area of UPLIFT is strengthening after-school care and support for students.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is done through school-based student care centres (SCCs) in Primary schools and after-school programmes in Secondary schools.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After-school support is especially important for students who do not have conducive home environments to return to after school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Providing these students with a structured and supervised after-school environment gives them the opportunity to develop good habits, routines and skills that will help them to succeed later in life.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since we started expanding school-based SCCs in 2012, we have increased the enrolment from 3,000 to about 27,000 this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We monitor demand for our SCCs closely and will work with the service providers to expand their capacity, but without compromising programme and service quality.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With more places in SCCs, we are now stepping up efforts to identify, enroll and provide support to students who would most benefit from SCCs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the past year, MOE worked closely with the community and MSF to study ground feedback, and walked the journey with these students and their families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We identified the main challenges that these families faced in enrolling their child in a SCC, and together, we developed solutions to address them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Making SCCs more affordable for low-income families is an important step towards getting these students into the SCCs and into the right environment for them to do well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim will share more about this in his speech for MSF later this week.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, some may require their children to head home after school to look after their younger siblings or grandparents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Others may need help with the documentation needed to apply for financial assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such complex challenges can only be surfaced and addressed through deeper, more personal, engagement with these families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Recognising this, we have developed a more comprehensive, proactive approach to reach out to families and tackle challenges together with them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, schools will proactively identify students who would benefit most from the SCC environment and then go the extra mile to engage and build trust with their families, encouraging them to enroll their child in the SCC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, we will engage the community to help address each family's challenges in a holistic and targeted way.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some families are referred to the Social Service Offices or Family Service Centres to help with childcare for their younger children, so that older ones can attend school and SCC, instead of having to look after their younger siblings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, teachers will walk families through the various documents that they have to submit and guide them through the process, if needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For families with complex circumstances, schools will exercise judgement and be more facilitative in the enrolment of children into the SCC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We piloted this outreach approach in a few Primary schools in July last year, because we wanted to see whether it would make a difference.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I was struck by the passion I saw in our teachers, who went out of their way to engage families, understand their challenges and work with the community to address them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They visited the students’ homes – multiple times in some cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After these students were enrolled, schools brought in community partners to engage them through targeted programmes to strengthen motivational support, resilience and holistic development.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, within the short span of six months, we have already begun to see progress in our students.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Boon Lay Garden Primary School, our pilot outreach efforts helped four siblings – let us call them Nadia, Adam, Sofia and Danial – to enrol in their school’s SCC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The four siblings received limited support at home, as their mother was busy taking care of three other younger siblings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think we are all familiar with cases like this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Adam and Danial, in particular, had longstanding difficulties with completing homework on time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since joining the school’s structured SCC environment, Adam and Danial have improved their time management skills and now manage their homework more confidently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the SCC at Boon Lay Garden is run by Big Heart Student Care, a joint venture by the four Self-Help Groups (SHGs), the brothers also enjoyed plug-in programmes run by the SHGs, like the "Backyard Science Workshops" run by MENDAKI.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The oldest sister, Nadia, also benefited from the SCC staff’s reinforcement of positive values and habits taught by the school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In recognition of her improvement, Nadia was awarded the school’s "Good Progress Award" last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With Nadia, Adam, Sofia and Danial progressing well in the SCC, their mother no longer needs to worry about them completing their homework when they return home.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will enable us to support more students from different backgrounds and further strengthen social mobility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about UPLIFT’s progress in partnering with community initiatives and how such initiatives could link up with UPLIFT.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since the Taskforce was set up, UPLIFT has been supporting collaboration between schools and the community.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am very encouraged by the number of people who have come up to me to say, "I want to be part of UPLIFT, how can I help?" It is not just individuals; community organisations and companies have come forward too, approaching the schools directly, or working through the UPLIFT Programme Office.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One such company is Singapore Press Holdings’ Chinese Media Group or CMG.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Leveraging their student publication, "Thumbs Up Junior", CMG staff including journalists and radio deejays engaged the students in enrichment activities and conversations, with the support of volunteers from the Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC) and Ngee Ann Polytechnic.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Apart from immersing students in a Chinese Language-rich environment and improving their fluency and confidence in the language, the journalists also shared about current affairs and their experiences, serving as positive role models for the students.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The students enjoy these interactions with their big brothers and sisters.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over time, we hope such programmes can help students hone	their strengths in their Mother Tongue Languages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As relationships deepen, the volunteers can also play a role in shaping the students’ aspirations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such mentorship opportunities can be valuable for students from disadvantaged backgrounds, as the mentors inspire them and broaden their worldview in a natural, informal setting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Another key focus area of UPLIFT is tackling long-term absenteeism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Early upstream intervention is critical to prevent occasional non-attendance from becoming long-term absenteeism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Earlier, I spoke about upcoming enhancements to SCC provisions for Primary school students.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: School-based support in SCCs and GEAR-UP can be complemented by community-based programmes like academic coaching, drop-in services and parenting support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, schools may not always know about these programmes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Likewise, community organisations may not always know which students and families need help.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To close this coordination gap, UPLIFT has worked closely with MSF to pilot a solution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Where students have emerging attendance issues and needs that can be met by community-based programmes, schools will refer them to the coordinator.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The coordinator will identify the needs of the students and their families, source for suitable resources and programmes offered by the local community partners, and then connect them to the students and families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By improving coordination, we can set up protective factors around the students and their families faster, and address underlying causes of absenteeism earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I hope that what I have shared today will inspire more individuals and organisations to step forward and	partner with us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Together, we can ensure that every Singaporean is cared for and supported to become the best that they can be.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is how we will build a society of opportunities for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, we started the SkillsFuture movement five years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The vision was to provide opportunities for all Singaporeans to develop skills mastery in different areas and fulfil our fullest potential regardless of our starting points in life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is what SkillsFuture is about – an inclusive and empowering national movement to enable all Singaporeans to chart our learning journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It starts from our schools, where we lay the foundation and passion for learning, followed by continuing education when students graduate and join the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This continues after we retire, as part of active ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like the inspiring story that Mr Murali Pillai shared, learning is a never-ending endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And as Ms Denise Phua has rightly pointed out, lifelong learning is a key focus for MOE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SkillsFuture provides the foundations to grow our economy, transform our enterprises, upskill our workers and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also enriches our lives as we learn new skills and discover new experiences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is an essential pillar for building a society which is both pro-enterprise and pro-worker, and	where	multiple	pathways	lead	to	multiple peaks	of excellence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We had three goals for the initial phase of SkillsFuture: to engender a shift in societal culture towards lifelong learning; to provide greater support for individuals to initiate and take ownership of their learning; to strengthen Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) as the third pillar of our CET ecosystem, complementing employers and private training providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many were able to perform their work better after training, and earned higher salaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Gan Thiam Poh on the need for quality control and risk management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to	ensure	the	quality	of	our	education	and	training ecosystem, to support courses with clear employability outcomes, and raise the quality bar for training providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since last year, SSG has enhanced its capabilities to deal with fraud and abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It set up a dedicated Division to focus on this area, and introduced data analytics and machine learning to detect suspicious claims, as well as more traditional methods, such as surprise checks and mystery shoppers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SSG will come down hard against errant training providers and individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Make no mistake – there will be zero tolerance for fraud and abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also review the legislation to further strengthen our regulatory and enforcement powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Two years ago, Minister Ong assessed that we were about a quarter of the way there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Recently, he said we have achieved close to 50%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: An improvement, but this is still only the halfway mark.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Advancing on the second half of our journey is what we want to achieve under the Next Bound of SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to focus on training that equip our workers with job relevant skills that enhance their employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In	particular,	we	want	employers	and	enterprises, especially SMEs, to play a bigger role in supporting lifelong learning and to upgrade the skills of their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, we will enhance support for individuals to initiate our own learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is important for Singaporeans who are self-employed and those who want to pursue a different career or learn a new skill beyond their current industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We	also	want	to	provide	more	help	for	mid-career Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s, to give them greater support to reskill and stay employable, whether is it in their current jobs, or if they switch to another company or industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The enhancements will be implemented under five areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, we will strengthen our collaborations with intermediaries to help enterprises with transformation and skills training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The better our skills training, the more assurance we can give to our workers and the	faster	we	can	transform	our	enterprises	and economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many	enterprises,	especially	SMEs,	do	not	have	the resources to conduct their own in-house training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Dr Intan asked about this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These anchor enterprises are industry leaders with deep sectoral knowledge, resources and extensive business networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is Singapore Power, which is working with SSG and eight SMEs in its supply chain to build workplace learning capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore Power aims to bring in another 40 SMEs by the end of this year, and eventually to include the rest of the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By having companies like Singapore Power train beyond their own needs, they can uplift the capabilities of other enterprises and also other workers in the entire sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I spoke about this yesterday at the MTI COS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SMEs can also benefit from many existing grants and subsidies to	improve	productivity,	redesign	jobs	and	train	their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Douglas Foo asked about training of emerging and future skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will tap on intermediaries such as TACs, anchor enterprises, IHLs and professional firms to provide guidance to employers on emerging skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, we will intensify efforts to help employers develop stronger workplace training capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The National Centre of Excellence for Workplace Learning (NACE) was launched at Nanyang Polytechnic in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: NACE has engaged over 250 companies for which 100 have started to implement workplace learning programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will expand NACE to two more IHLs over the next few years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The next one will be at the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We launched the first slate of SkillsFuture Work-Study Programmes in 2015, with close links to the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Students can apply what they learnt in school to their workplaces and bring practical experiences and problem statements from their jobs back to the classrooms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Employers welcome the programme as it helps them to attract more young Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Work-Study	Programmes	are	useful	to	prepare	our students for the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But	applied	learning	is	not	confined	to	Work-Study Programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Faisal Manap suggested having a national level framework to establish common standards in internships and facilitate matching of students to internships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This was one of the recommendations by the Applied Study in Polytechnics and ITE Review (ASPIRE) Committee chaired by Second Minister Indranee Rajah.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IHLs would ensure that their students on internships are provided with structured mentorship from the participating companies, with clear learning outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 90% of Polytechnic students undergo structured credit-bearing internships in their final year of diploma studies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And these cover a wide range of industries, including culinary, retail, hospitality, healthcare and early childhood education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, it was not factually accurate for Mr Faisal Manap to say that internships are mostly for technology and finance sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the matching of students to internships, a centralised model, as suggested by Mr Faisal Manap, may not produce better outcomes than the current approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The way companies currently offer internships is through partnerships with our IHLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The	IHLs	know	their	students	well	and	what	industry opportunities are needed to deepen their learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, it is not quite the same as companies filling job vacancies through open recruitment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The two process may appear same-same, but they are different.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The SkillsFuture Credit was introduced in 2015 to bring about an important mindset change, that each of us must take charge of our personal learning journey towards skills mastery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than half a million Singaporeans have used their Credit and amongst them, close to 40% have either fully used up their Credit, or are close to doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if some workers could start using the top-up before 1 October.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The	SkillsFuture	Credit	top-up	is	designed	to	support individuals with their lifelong learning needs beyond the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is why the top-up is valid for five years, till 31 December 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The original start date was 1 January 2021, but SSG has done what it could to bring it forward to 1 October 2020, while ensuring that the top-ups are administered accurately and used appropriately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SSG will look at the possibility of allowing appeals on a case- by-case basis, for example, for those who are in-between jobs and need to use their Credit for training to get a new job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For individuals who are currently employed, we encourage their employers to provide them with the training during this period, tapping	on	the	Absentee	Payroll	and	training	subsidies provided by SSG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The employees can then keep their SkillsFuture Credit for use later, within that five-year window.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat spoke about training support for mature freelancers and he made reference to the Surrogate Employer Programme which Mr Patrick Tay mentioned during Budget debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Those who are aged 40 and above can receive further subsidies of up to 90% under the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Enhanced Subsidy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It does not matter if they are employees, self-employed or in between jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For employees who are sent for training by their companies, their employers will typically cover the post-subsidy course fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For others, like freelancers, they would pay the 10% co-payment on their own, and they can use their SkillsFuture Credit for the out-of-pocket costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, contrary to what Mr Png said yesterday, self-employed persons and freelancers aged 40 and above will receive up to 90% in course fee subsidy, no different from an employee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this includes courses for freelance trainers, which Mr Png mentioned in his cut.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Png also made reference to the Surrogate Employer Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Patrick Tay had raised this idea in the context of providing a training allowance to self-employed persons while they go for training, to help them during the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is different from the SkillsFuture course fee subsidy that I explained earlier, which is not linked to the Surrogate Employer Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The 90% course fee subsidy is one thing, the training allowance is another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Ms Foo Mee Har on the need to support individuals in navigating the courses available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will provide customised recommendations on training options through MySkillsFuture portal, including quality and outcomes ratings of courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we hope this will help individuals to decide which courses will be more relevant or have better quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For individuals who prefer face-to-face support, we have been working with the libraries, CDCs, e2i and PA, to provide SkillsFuture Advice workshops to help individuals find out about different SkillsFuture initiatives and plan for their training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 100,000 individuals have participated in these workshops, and even more will benefit in the years ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are planning to expand the reach and enhance the training guidance under SkillsFuture Advice	via the Career Centres, in collaboration with partners like the unions and career advisors, including private sector entities that provide such services on a commercial basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this will supplement the assistance for individuals provided through	the portal and our existing SkillsFuture Advice workshops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will help them to refresh and rejuvenate their skill-sets, so that they can remain employable and benefit from new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Deputy Prime Minister announced a comprehensive set of measures under the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The other Ministries – MTI, MCI, MOM – have touched on some of these initiatives yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOE will work with MOM and MTI to increase capacity and placements for re-skilling programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We	will	ramp	up	the	capacity	for	career	transition programmes at CET centres, to complement other re-skilling programmes such as Professional Conversion, Place-and-Train and Tech Skills Accelerator Mid-Career Advance for ICT jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked if these career transition programmes could be more targeted at mid-career workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, many of the re-skilling programmes are, what we call Place-and-Train, where individuals are first matched with an employer before they start their training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will add to these by expanding the career transition programmes, as suggested by Dr Lim Wee Kiak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Individuals will be trained before they receive career support services, such as advisory and placement from CET centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is less certainty of placement compared to Place-and-Train, but this provides greater flexibility in the eventual choice of job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also allows us to train more individuals in industry-relevant skills to enhance their employment prospects and offer employers a job-ready candidate at the point of placement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Both types of programmes have their usefulness and their relevance as they serve different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From 2020, these different re-skilling programmes will collectively increase the placements of Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If he has not used his first $500 from 2015, he will have a total amount of $1,500.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the Next Bound of SkillsFuture, we target to benefit a total of 28,000 companies and one million individuals over the next five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will need more resources to support these enhancements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are investing even more in SkillsFuture compared to the first five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, we have to review our existing initiatives, and reallocate our resources across different areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will review course subsidy rates, together with the Enhanced Subsidy Schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to subsidise up to 90%, with more support for courses that lead to clearer employment outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is in line with the calls from several Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also be making some adjustments to Absentee Payroll.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The larger enterprises are currently benefiting more from this provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will review the rates and set a maximum amount each company can receive so that the funding support can be distributed to more companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We were planning to make these changes together with the enhancements under the Next Bound of SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, with the COVID-19 situation, we will defer these changes to a later date and focus our efforts for now to help businesses and workers to tide through the current challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The intent is to help our companies and workers during this difficult period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And as Deputy Prime Minister said, if the situation calls for it, the Government is prepared to do more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the appeal process for PSEA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We had discussed the usage of PSEA in this House in November last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And Ms Lim is right that PSEA monies are not subsidies per se, but they comprise mainly Government top-ups which come from public funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have a responsibility to safeguard the interests of all account holders by upholding the quality and relevance of approved courses, to guide Singaporeans on which courses would produce better outcomes for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I understand Ms Lim's point in the case of her resident, due to his unfortunate family situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will share her feedback with MOE colleagues to see how we can improve the appeals process for handling exceptional cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   SkillsFuture will continue to be a critical enabler for Singapore's next phase of development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It supports skills training and lifelong learning, and it can help enterprises transform and be more competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have made good progress with SkillsFuture in the past five years, and will be taking it into the next bound.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The top-up will be valid for five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will benefit employers and provide more pathways and options for our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In English	): Mr Chairman, MOE is committed to building a strong foundation for students in schools and also offering a quality education at the IHLs and lifelong learning thereafter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister and Second Minister covered the initiatives in schools earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our IHLs have similarly embraced the spirit of recognising aptitudes, skills and experience over qualifications and translated this philosophy into their admission policies, enhancing porosity across the different pathways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister and Second Minister covered the initiatives in schools earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our IHLs have, similarly, embraced the spirit of recognising aptitudes, skills and experience over qualifications, and translated this philosophy into their admissions policies, enhancing porosity across the different pathways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, for "A" Level students who do not progress to the AUs, we will help them obtain a Polytechnic Diploma within a shorter time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we will expand aptitude-based admissions at NUS, NTU and SMU.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This enables more students to be considered based on non-academic aptitudes and strengths, and broadens holistic recognition of individuals beyond grades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we will expand pathways for working adults to enrol in full-time diploma courses, including those who have part-time Nitec, Higher Nitec or WSQ diploma qualifications and we will do so by recognising their relevant work experiences and the skills that they have acquired.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These changes in higher education reflect the spirit of SkillsFuture to provide multiple pathways, support continuous learning and deepen our focus on skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are part of MOE’s effort to build a continuum of education and learning opportunities for every Singaporean, starting from young, through our adult and working life, and after we retire, as part of active ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Let us work together to build a nation of lifelong learners with a deep passion for new knowledge and skills; to grow a society that values skills mastery and recognises different peaks of excellence; and to nurture a people who are resilient and resourceful, and who are ready to seize the opportunities that come our way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, as I hear about how we are supporting our people to seize the opportunities of the future, I am reminded of the importance of nurturing well-rounded individuals guided by a strong set of values.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: That said, I am also reminded how important it is for all of us – parents, teachers, and the community – to work together to bring out the best in our children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to first speak in Malay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   Over the last few years, many parents have shared with me that being a parent has brought them tremendous joy – but equally, many sleepless nights.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As a father of two children, I can relate to this sentiment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As parents, we want what is best for our children and seek to bring out the best in them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, we are also responsible for moulding them into responsible individuals with a strong moral compass, a sense of heritage, and as Minister Ong had shared earlier – a strong foundation of values, tools and skills to navigate the world ahead of them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is also something that MOE is committed to – even as we embark on the shifts in our education system that my colleagues have spoken about.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Cheng Li Hui and Mr Seah Kian Peng asked about our partnerships with parents, community, and industry, and how these would help to nurture the right values, dispositions, and skills in our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, our schools actively reach out to parents, and work closely with them to support our children in pursuing their strengths and interests, and to impart good values and attitudes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I was very encouraged when Madam Titek Rohani, whose youngest child is now in secondary school, shared how she makes it a point to learn from teachers about her child’s strengths and interests, her child’s relationships with fellow students, and whether her child contributes to his peers’ learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: She also works closely with the school to guide her child as he explores different education pathways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, second, schools and parents work closely to role model good values and attitudes for our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Values are both caught and taught, and likewise both practised and preached.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am very heartened to hear how parents and teachers are collectively encouraging and galvanising students amidst the COVID-19 virus situation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They are indeed role models for our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our teachers have seized the opportunity to educate our students about the virus and their part to play.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They do this through teaching scientific knowledge; inculcating good hygiene practices; as well as facilitating discussions on empathy, resilience, and a sense of community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Parents too, have volunteered their time and effort to support the school community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, Rulang Primary School had sent out a circular to parents to inform them of the extra cleaning measures undertaken to ensure that the premises remained clean.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In response, members of the Parent Support Group volunteered to help with cleaning efforts, which reduced the load of frontline support staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition, the parents put together care packages to encourage the staff, cleaners and security officers for their hard work in ensuring that the school premises remained clean and safe.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: From both our teachers and parents, our students are learning how they too can be part of the solution: by demonstrating kindness and being socially responsible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Together, they demonstrate the resilient, caring spirit of partnership that binds the nation together in trying times.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Lastly, community and industry partners have a big role to play in developing our students holistically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our schools have been actively engaging them to provide a richer learning experience for our students and broaden their horizons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Terence Ho asked what our plans were for developing local arts institutions and suggested introducing local composers and compositions as part of our music curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Some schools have gone further and engaged local artistes to contribute to their programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, Boon Lay Secondary School works closely with industry practitioners – such as Ms Melissa Quek, who is the Head of the School of Dance and Theatre at the LaSalle College of the Arts – to plan and deliver dance lessons/workshops under the school’s Learning for Life Programme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This partnership has inspired students to appreciate the arts more deeply, and exposed them to different career possibilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, I would also like to take this chance to reaffirm the Government's commitment to supporting our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked if we would extend subsidies for Primary school students with foreign passports.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Likewise, Singaporean students in MOE-funded schools who need financial support are eligible for financial assistance schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Nonetheless, non- citizen students with at least one Singaporean or Permanent Resident parent can approach our schools for assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will assess their situations and exercise flexibility on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap asked if we would extend the Financial Assistance Scheme and Edusave Award to full- time madrasah students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He drew a parallel with the provision of Edusave Contributions (EC) to madrasah students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This ensures every Singapore Citizen child receives support for secular enrichment activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Edusave Awards, by contrast, is part of the programme in our national schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They recognise the character, leadership, conduct, learning dispositions, and academic achievements of students enrolled in national schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Similarly, the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme caters to students in MOE-funded schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: That said, the Government recognises the role that the madrasahs play for the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Furthermore, PROMAS recipients who perform well in both their religious and secular subjects and exhibit exemplary character are also eligible for the PROMAS Performance Award.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, in closing, I would like to reiterate that it is only through our collective efforts – with parents, teachers, and the community – that we bring out the best in our children and nurture well-rounded individuals guided by a strong set of values.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While we may play different roles, we can all work together, as MOE’s mission statement proclaims, "to mould the future of our nation".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, a teacher once told me and, I quote, "Our job is not to prepare students for something.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our job is to help students prepare themselves for anything." And I thought this is really true and this captures the essence of what MOE seeks to do as we enable Singaporeans to "Learn for Life", as what Minister Ong Ye Kung has shared in his speech earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To put Singaporeans in a good stead for the future, like what Minister Ong said earlier, proficiency in Mother Tongue Languages (MTL) is key, as the age of Asia opens door to greater opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, please allow me to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, the learning of our Mother Tongue Languages (MTL) is only natural given our cultural context, and will also help our students grasp the opportunities of a rising Asia.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since then, we have worked closely with the community to encourage the learning of MTL within and beyond schools – be it Chinese, Tamil, or Malay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Over the last few years, there has been a stronger nexus between the work of the Committees and the formal MTL curriculum, and this has led to a mutually reinforcing relationship between schools and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Teachers and students are encouraged to apply lessons from the classroom to their daily lives and creations, to support joyful and authentic MTL learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For instance, Members may be familiar with the annual National School "Xinyao" Festival.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Instead of just singing a song that is composed by others, students would have to draw inspiration from the textbook and compose a new song.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last year, I attended the finals which lasted for about three hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It was fascinating and we were deeply impressed by the students’ creativity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Two sisters composed, performed, and produced a music video for a song titled "华佗" (Huatuo), inspired by the tale of a renowned physician in their Chinese textbook.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Those of us who read Chinese martial arts novels would be familiar with “Huatuo".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The catchy tune and accessible lyrics of the song allow the story to shine through to the youth and enable a better understanding of not only Huatuo, but also traditional Chinese medicine and the essence of Chinese culture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will release this video in the near future and I encourage all of you to watch it, and share it with your family and friends.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: There are many wonderful examples that can be drawn from this competition.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Like the sisters, many of our students’ work have been reproduced as useful lesson materials for our teachers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We believe that the collective energy and support of schools, families, the media, the entertainment circle, and the larger community, will sustain a vibrant ecosystem to ignite students' interest and love for their MTL, be it Chinese, Tamil, or Malay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, Sir, please allow me to also share examples of the work of our Malay and Tamil Language Learning Promotion Committees in making MTL learning relatable, in making MTL learning enjoyable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This programme allows our students to learn the language in the context of coding application and software and then apply it in novel and also technological settings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I am confident that the committees will continue to bring together the passion, the creativity and energy of our schools, parents, media and the community to sustain a vibrant eco-system for students to like, to learn and to use their MTL as living languages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, apart from reinforcing our bilingual foundations, MOE is also committed to developing the whole child through a broad-based and holistic curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Secondary school students, for example, will learn in Geography lessons the effects of climate change on our food supply chain and also the forests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In Science, they will investigate how human activities disrupt the carbon cycle, contribute to climate change and threaten our environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As part of the curriculum development process, we also consult MEWR and other relevant authorities to provide our students with the most up-to-date and accurate information on climate change.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More importantly, we hone our students' ability in discerning the news and also engage them in inquiry-based learning and discussion so that our students are guided to examine different sources of information critically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Beyond the classroom, many schools have programmes that partner the community to promote environmental causes and give our students the chance to translate their knowledge into action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As part of their training, they go through modules on the environment like energy efficiency and climate change, as well as the 4Rs that we are all very familiar with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The 4Rs are to Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and most recently, to Refuse.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This further instils in our students, green practices and mind-sets like waste minimisation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Many Members are very active on the ground, in the community; you will agree with me that students are our best ambassadors, because when they go back and tell their mummy, daddy or grandparents, "You forgot to switch off the aircon, you forgot to switch off the lights", I think the whole family will remember the green practices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, we are counting on our students to really spread the word for us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The other CDCs are also implementing similar green initiatives with the schools in their districts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As part of our on-going efforts to redefine CCA experiences, MOE is also exploring how to better promote social mixing and inclusivity through CCAs, as advocated by Ms Cheng.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In time to come, we believe our CCA experiences will better support our students' holistic growth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, to conclude, I recap the educator's quote that I started with, "Our job is not to prepare students for something.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our job is to help students prepare themselves for anything".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
