text: Yes, we should help our students prepare themselves for anything that may come their way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In so doing, we will raise a generation of Singaporeans with a sense of confidence over their lives and their future, no matter what uncertainties a changing world may hold.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, MOE will continue to work with stakeholders to nurture our youths to become active citizens with a love to Learn for Life, and willing to act for a better Singapore that we collectively own.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Just a few questions on Tree for Life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: First, on my suggestion to rename or consider the idea of Ministry of Education being the Ministry of Lifelong Learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat just mentioned that MOE is now providing a continuum of learning opportunities for Singaporeans for the entire life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I thought that a new name might reflect better MOE's new vision and mission.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Also, education somehow, smacks of a one-way flow: of I educate you, I teach you; versus the idea of self-driven learning whereby the ownership is put on the people who are learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: My second question is on the transformation map.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: It will be great, if in this so-called transformation map in the form of a tree, the types of fruit could be articulated better in terms of what kind of students you want to see; what kind of learners; and what kind of desired outcomes, including how we will benchmark – my point which Minister maybe forgot to respond to – benchmark what would be the success of our education system versus the usual ones that we are quite used to – PISA rankings and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The next is the ground in the graphic of Tree for Life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For the ground, we could specify the foundational principles by which our uniquely Singapore education system should aspire towards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Principles like equal access, and a lot of the things that are already being done in our country, like being inclusive, like being collaborative, like always looking at future-proofing and looking ahead.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Those could be the foundational principles that occupy the ground from which this tree grows.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The third is in terms of the branches in the Tree for Life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I thought that many of the things that Ministers, Senior Minister of State and Senior Parliamentary Secretaries have mentioned are to do with enablers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: How we look at the future roles of staff, be they education leaders or educators, the curriculum, the content to teach, the pedagogy by which we teach.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: These are great enablers that can be considered as the branches.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And then, there is also the weather condition.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Beyond the Tree per se – but the conditions on how we are all conditioned to think of as, like a certain way, when we look at education in our country; and some of the driving forces to support what MOE is trying to do —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Denise Phua, can you keep it to clarification, instead of another speech?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There are physical devices but we need therapists, coach services too.

speaker: The Chairman
text: How many supplementary questions are there, Ms Denise Phua?

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you can just keep it succinct, please.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Because they just need that longer runway to enable them to be more independent in daily living and to allow them to perhaps have a better chance to do some supported employment work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the analogy of a tree cannot be pushed too far, but that is always the danger when you use an analogy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Foundational principles – I totally agree with Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we came up with this "Tree for Life" and the Learn for Life movement, we were focusing on the deltas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What are the main changes we want to make.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One example is UPLIFT, which is something that we are putting a lot more resources to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But surely, all the principles that the Member mentioned earlier – they continue to be relevant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But this tree is focusing on the delta.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned in my speech, it will guide us in our actions for the next five to 10 years – the key changes that we want to see in the system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member's points on the branches, on the different kinds of fruits – actually, if we want students of different abilities to have different pathways, one fruit is not enough.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You need a whole orchard of different kinds of fruits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, again, the analogy cannot be taken too far.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I take all of the Member's points.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why I say the education system must always be a work in progress.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we say we have a plan for the next five to 10 years, I am sure along the way, there will be new initiatives, new imperatives and we have to change again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will leave the Second Minister to answer the question on SEN, but on the renaming to the Ministry for Lifelong Learning – we agree with the essence of what the Member said.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the essence of what the Member wishes MOE will do, we will do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we do it well, we achieve what we want to do, and promote lifelong learning the way we want to, at that point in time, maybe we can think about a change of our name.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I need to respond to Ms Denise Phua's many supplementary questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first clarification Ms Denise Phua had was – how come it is $5,000 for the SEN Fund for those with social and behavioural conditions instead of $25,000?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, for the assistive devices, they may need an assistive learning system, talking calculators, reader pens.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those are generally more expensive than other types of devices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You may need somebody to do sign language and then you obviously have to cover that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And for the blind students, sometimes you need note-taking services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is scoped depending on the need and basically, for hearing loss and visual impairment, the cost of the devices and support is higher.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the high-needs category may not be so applicable to them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this much I can assure Ms Denise Phua, which is that MOE will continue to work with our IHLs and we will review the SEN Fund periodically.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our ultimate aim is to ensure that the students with SEN are adequately supported with the necessary devices that they need.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Denise Phua also made a passionate plea for us to keep some of the students in the SPED schools for longer, up to age 21.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, there are two things that we are doing, which will partially address that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I agree that there is much more that we can look at, to see how we can support those who leave school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, let me just take them in turn.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first thing is, MOE has already started in the SPED schools a school-wide process of transition planning for all the SPED students at the Secondary age.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The school has developed an individual transition plan for each student, working with the students, the care-givers and the family, and the idea is really to help them to be able to cope when they leave school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is the first thing, and this will apply to all the SPED students, irrespective of whether or not they may be able to go into open employment, or not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is number one – prepare them all for when they leave school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While on the programme, the students receive customised job training, job support from job coaches to prepare them for eventual employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, I think Ms Denise Phua's concern really is that there may be some who are not able to do open employment and her appeal is, can we keep them in the school system?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But even if we did that, even up to age 21, there are still some, who, after age 21, still cannot cope with open employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think what Ms Denise Phua wants to do is to sort of lengthen the runway.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think we have spent the last decade or so really ensuring that SPED is strengthened, that we have got good quality in terms of the content as well as the teachers and those who can provide the programmes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you can see we are now taking the next step, which is helping them to transition beyond school and those who can go to open employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think I can say this – we agree that that is certainly an area that has to be looked into, for those who cannot go into open employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Work in progress, and we will be very happy to partner all the stakeholders in this space to come up and see what is the best thing for them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It may or may not be retaining them in school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But what we really want is that no matter what it is, when you leave SPED school, you also want those with special needs to be able to live lives which are as productive as possible, and which also gives their care-givers a sense of assurance, that their loved ones with special needs are engaged and have something to do, and are in an environment which is conducive for them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I have two questions for the Senior Minister of State on SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: First, thank you for very much for the range of exciting initiatives on SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The first clarification I have is that I ask the Senior Minister of State how the next phase of SkillsFuture movement will bring about a closer link between the CET courses and employability.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I spoke about the challenge amongst the thousands of courses and people needed help to navigate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: What skills do I have to achieve based on the CET courses offered that would link me to a very good employment outcome, especially those 40 to 60 years old, the same group we are trying to help.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The second clarification I have for the Senior Minister of State is on the SkillsFuture Queen Bee initiative.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: It is a very exciting initiative and there were so very impressive numbers being mentioned, that SMEs are being brought on board.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I asked in my speech if the Senior Minister of State can give more details about how this new model works, maybe specifically give some details on the governance, the funding, whether there is any certification involved, so that some of the skills can be portable.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, just really going a bit deeper about if these Queen Bees are going to be schools of the industries, how are they going to be governed, how are they going to be funded, and the quality control about the programmes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Ms Foo Mee Har for her two supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the first, she is right that because we offer so many different kinds of courses, it is useful for people to get some advisory, some guidance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If I take this course, what are some of the pathways that may be open to me?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What are some of the outcomes that I can benefit from?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is going to be done through two channels, mainly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will be in collaboration with MOM, Workforce Singapore and also with our unions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And as I mentioned earlier, also with private sector entities that can come in and provide some of these advisory services on a commercial basis.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Through this process, we hope to be able to supplement the support that we give to individuals and help them to make those decisions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And that is also what we will do in the next bound – to further raise the quality of the training providers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is going to be one of the key priorities too.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Foo Mee Har's second question on Queen Bees.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have lined up some companies but every sector is different.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some Queen Bees, like in the case of SP Group, are there because they have many links with suppliers and contractors in the sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, they are able to then influence what these SMEs do.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because these SMEs, many of them are their suppliers, their contractors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in some cases, it is not quite like that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The people who are participating and the SMEs may not be direct contractors or suppliers, but they are part of the industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the model needs to be customised depending on which Queen Bee company we are working with, which sector we are working on.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I think the fundamental principle remains that what we want is to be able to have these Queen Bee companies to take the lead and work with us as partners, to be able to raise the training opportunities and resources available to other companies and workers within the sector.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: The second is a comment on the device ownership scheme.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: I appreciate that there are many virtues to personal device usage in schools, but there are also certain pitfalls that we need to think about.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: Previous research has shown that device ownership actually involves many components, including device purchase, device maintenance, software maintenance as well as software usage.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: And families are clearly differently advantaged in being able to provide the guidance.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: So, I have found in my own research that parents from less well-heeled backgrounds face severe inadequacy and severe anxiety in terms of their inability to support their children in this way.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: In other words, unless we have very concerted, very comprehensive support and augmentation within schools for IT support for students from different backgrounds, you may find that some of these introductions of device usage may introduce different kinds of inequalities.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun
text: So, I hope due attention can be paid to this issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun talked about microaggression yesterday.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not deny that sometimes it can happen, but I do not think it is so widespread that we have to roll out a national training programme for our teachers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over time, as they gain experience, they will have more patience and have the skills to handle difficult situations as opposed to losing their cool.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think actually all of us need those kind of skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it does not mean we get angry all the time.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I seek your kind indulgence for four clarifications.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: First, I support the National Digital Literacy programme but, as I mentioned in my speech, Minister, I hope that MOE will consider including information literacy as well because it is not sufficient for students to just learn to develop skills and knowledge to make use of digital tools and platforms but also understand how to navigate the massive amounts of information available that traverses all these various digital tools and platforms.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Second, for the SkillsFuture for educators, I understand that MOE will be working with NIE as well as private training providers, external training providers, for both in-service and pre-service courses, and which may also include online learning modules.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Will this be fully funded by MOE or will teachers have to tap on the SkillsFuture Credit, for example?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Third, I have not spoken it in this Committee of Supply but I have spoken about this before.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It is good that we are strengthening the support for students with SEN in our schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Are there plans to recruit more AED(LBS) because at the moment, there are only one or two AED(LBS) to cater to 80% of our students with special educational needs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I hope that there will be a lot more AED(LBS) because it will certainly help our students with special education needs in the mainstream schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: And, last, the expansion of the intake places for Work Study programmes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I must declare that I am from SIT as a faculty member.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: SIT was the first to start the Work-Study programmes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar

text: Yes, as I mentioned, the four components of digital literacy simplified – Find, Think, Apply, Create.

text: One important modality for teachers when they learn is to do so in a professional community, learning from each other.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I am very heartened and I also thank both Ministers for their resounding assurances that we are finally introducing mental health education in schools, and also that MOE will be providing more and better trained counsellors to schools.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot agree more with Minister Indranee that we need a whole child and whole school and an ecosystem to address students' mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The first one is that a clear big piece within this eco-system in addressing students' well-being, mental well-being, particularly, would be the parents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am wondering how and when are parents engaged by the schools for a student in distress, and also if we are including parents in the mental health education that we are introducing in some way.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also wonder if one way could be reaching these parents through their employers and that there might be an inter-Ministry initiative with MOM, given the announcement in terms of the Workplace Mental Health Advisory.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The second clarification is, does the Ministry have, or if not, does it intend to have a clear and robust Suicide Prevention strategy in schools, especially given the record number of teenage suicides that we had in 2018 that was announced last year?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Member is correct that the parents are actually a very important part of this, and our teachers do engage the parents, especially when the teachers find that their child has a mental health issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the plan to engage parents is very much a part of it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When the Member refers to a suicide prevention strategy, actually, that strategy is the peer support network or the programme that I talked about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because in my speech, I had outlined how it is actually a whole eco-system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If a child is depressed, worried, the first people to pick it up will be the friends, the friends are the first ones.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if it is not too big an issue, the friends can provide support, then that is great.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if it needs a little bit more than that, then you would want to bring it to the attention of the teacher.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the teacher can resolve it, that is fine, but if not, you may have to go to the professional counsellor.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And then, from the counsellor, you may have to go to specialised external service providers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, you can see that it is one layer after another layer, but all to have a protective environment around a student who has got mental health issues.
